terms.gloss: Do you have …? Have you got …?
evidence: Mart. 4.72.2: Nōn habeō, sed habet bibliopōla Tryphōn.
Levi–Bini p. 267: Opera omnia Vergiliī. Habēsne? — Habeō.
terms.comment: Habēre is used of what a seller has in his shop, as of Martial’s bookseller. The answer repeats the verb: Habeō, or Nōn habeō.

terms.grammar: ecquid with a partitive genitive, or ecquem, ecquam, ecquōs agreeing with the thing asked for
evidence: Plaut. Pers. 225: Ecquid habēs? — Ecquid tū?
terms.comment: The livelier question: whether there is any at all. Lewis & Short calls ecquis a word of impassioned questions.

evidence: Mart. 1.117.8: Quod quaeris propius petās licēbit.
terms.comment: What the buyer says, and what the seller answers when he has found it: En quod quaeris, “here’s what you’re looking for”. For the verb see “look for”.

phrases.latin: Habēsne calceōs puerīlēs? — Habeō; quantōs quaeris?
phrases.english: Do you have children’s shoes? — I do; what size are you after?
I’m looking for a winter cap; have you got one?

phrases.latin: Exigis ut dōnem nostrōs tibi, Quīnte, libellōs. Nōn habeō, sed habet bibliopōla Tryphōn.
phrases.english: You ask me to give you my books, Quintus. I haven’t any, but Tryphon the bookseller has.

phrases.latin: Opera omnia Vergiliī. Habēsne? — Habeō; sed annotāta vīs annōn?
phrases.english: The complete works of Virgil. Do you have them? — I do; but do you want them with notes or not?

sources: Lewis & Short: habeo · Lewis & Short: ecquis · Lewis & Short: quaero
Enrico Levi and Arturo Bini, Il latino come lingua viva (1937), p. 267.
